references.text: The promise of a land flowing with milk and honey was first given to Moses at the burning bush.
The description of the promised land as flowing with milk and honey is repeated in connection with the exodus from Egypt.
God calls Israel a stiff-necked people after the golden calf incident; the same expression is used here.
Moses acknowledges that the people are stiff-necked and asks for God's forgiveness and presence.
Moses reminds the people that they are a stiff-necked people.
God repeats to Moses that this people is stiff-necked.
The promise of the land flowing with milk and honey is confirmed before entering Canaan.
God threatens to destroy the people because of their disobedience, a warning similar to this one.
Stephen calls the Jews stiff-necked in his speech, referencing Israel's history.
Contrast between God's threat to deny the journey to the promised land due to sin and the people who complained that they never got to enter it.
Ezekiel confirms historically and theologically that God's threat in Exodus 33 not to lead the people into the land was fulfilled for the wilderness generation.
The original promise of the journey to the promised land (Ex 3:17) stands in direct contrast to the threat to cut short the journey because of the people's sin (Ex 33:3).
